## Skills

*	Explain the purpose of a multiple comparison procedure to compare multiple means.
* Be able to identify a situation that requires ANOVA.  
    + Identify the factor (i.e. explanatory variable) and response variable.  
    + Be able to state the appropriate hypotheses for ANOVA.  
    + Report ANOVA results in an ANOVA table and be able to interpret each part of the table within the context of the study.  
* Explain the necessary conditions to use an ANOVA  
    + Be able to assess the conditions.  
* Be able to identify a situation that requires an ANOVA for transformed data
    + Identify the factor (i.e. explanatory variable) and response variable
    + Be able to state the appropriate verbal-only hypotheses for a transformed ANOVA
    + Report ANOVA results in an ANOVA table and be able to interpret each part of the table within the context of the study.
* Be able to interpret output from a post hoc test (Tukey's method).
* Be able to explain the difference between multiple t-tests and a post hoc test.
* Be able to execute the proper R codes to conduct ANOVA and post hoc analyses.

The above skills cover LT 1-5, 10-11, 13, 15-16, 18, 21, 23-24.  It also introduces R-LT R7 and reviews R-LTs R1-R2.

## Scenario 1: Cuckoo Egg Length        

Common cuckoos (*Cuculus canorus*) are brood parasites, meaning that they lay their eggs in the nests of host species, where they are adopted and hatched by the host birds. Once the cuckoo chick hatches, it pushes the host's eggs or young out of the nest, monopolizing the feeding of the typically small host parents to the typically larger cuckoo chick. Prior to the chick hatching, however, the cuckoo egg needs to be accepted by the host species as one of their own, despite large differences in size between the roughly pigeon sized adult cuckoo and the wide variety of sizes of the host (smaller than sparrows to larger than robins). The variety in size of the host species are mirrored in a variety of sizes in the eggs of those species. 

Cuckoo eggs vary in size and coloration. Researchers are interested in determining why that might be. They think that egg size might depend on either the size of the mother laying the egg, or possibly on the host species (to help the cuckoo egg be adopted). Data were collected by observing a random sample of known cuckoo territories. Researchers monitored each selected cuckoo pair for indications the female was ready to lay an egg. They then followed the female during all daylight hours when she was active to record any laying event. Researchers collect data on the maternal size, host nest species, and the length of the egg, in mm. Maternal size was classified into three sizes, since the observed laying mother was not disturbed to collect and measure her length; instead size was classified from photographs as small, medium and large. Researchers collected data from eggs laid in the host nest of five species: tree pipits, hedge sparrows, robins, wagtails, and wrens. The data are found in `cuckoo_egg-length.csv`.

**Researchers want to examine if there is a difference in the cuckoo egg size depending on the species of the host nest.**

### Scenario 2: Impulse Rates of Molluscs      


Scientists at Hopkins Marine Station in Monterey, CA questioned why an aquatic snail moves slower than a slug and much slower than a squid, even though these three are molluscs (Molluscs are organisms that belong to the same phylum). They wonder if this is due to sodium channels, proteins that start electrical nerve impulses. Do slower molluscs have slower-acting sodium channels than faster molluscs (and thus slower electrical nerve impulses for movement)? The scientists collected a total of 118 specimens from random locations near Monterey Bay. Each specimen is either a *Pleurobranchaea californica* (sea slug), *Limax maximus* (leopard snail), or a *Loligo pealii* (Longfin inshore Squid). They took the nervous systems of the specimens and grew their nerve cells in culture for electrical studies. They then used a patch clamp to detect the reaction of sodium channels to small changes in voltage. They recorded the species and the impulse rate (cm/s) of each specimen in the data set `mollusc.csv`.

**Researchers want to determine if the nervous impulse rate of molluscs differs between species (that move at different speeds).**
